name: Naltrexone/Bupropion ER (Contrave)
summary: Prescription weight-loss medication that combines naltrexone (opioid blocker) + bupropion (dopamine/norepinephrine antidepressant). Psych-relevant because it can affect mood, anxiety, sleep, and suicidality risk—especially early on or with dose changes.
description: Contrave is FDA-approved for chronic weight management—not for depression, anxiety, or any psychiatric disorder. But it contains bupropion, which can rev up energy, worsen insomnia, increase jitteriness, and (rarely) flip people into agitation or mania. It also contains naltrexone, which blocks opioids and can trigger opioid withdrawal if you’re not opioid-free. Biggest psych safety headline: monitor closely for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, especially in younger adults and during dose changes.
patient_summary: Contrave is for weight management—not for depression or anxiety. Psych-wise, it can change sleep, anxiety, irritability, and mood (especially in the first 1-2 months or when the dose is adjusted). If you have bipolar risk, seizure risk, an eating disorder history, uncontrolled blood pressure, or you use opioids, this med can be a bad fit. If mood gets darker or suicidal thoughts show up, treat that as urgent—not “just side effects.”

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Combination: Opioid Antagonist (naltrexone) + NDRI antidepressant (bupropion), Extended-Release

primary_indications: Chronic weight management (adjunct to reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity) in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related comorbidity

linked_conditions.context: Sometimes considered in psychiatric practice when weight gain/metabolic risk is worsened by psych meds (especially if preferred weight-loss agents aren’t options). Not FDA-approved for antipsychotic-associated weight gain, and psychiatric side effects (insomnia, anxiety, agitation, mood shifts) can limit tolerability.

May be discussed when cravings/reward-driven eating is a major problem, but it is not FDA-approved for binge eating disorder. Screen carefully for eating disorder history, bipolar risk, and seizure risk.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to bupropion, naltrexone, or any component
Concomitant use of other bupropion-containing products (including, but not limited to: Wellbutrin, Wellbutrin SR, Wellbutrin XL, Aplenzin, Zyban)
Chronic opioid use, opioid agonist therapy (eg, methadone), or partial agonist therapy (eg, buprenorphine)
Seizure disorder or history of seizures
Current or past diagnosis of bulimia or anorexia nervosa
Patients undergoing abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, antiseizure drugs
Concomitant use of MAOIs or use within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
Initiation in a patient receiving linezolid or IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.comparison_data: If weight loss is <4% to 5% of baseline after ~3 months on therapy, consider discontinuation
efficacy_response.patient_text: This med has a built-in reality check: if you’re not down about 4-5% of your starting weight after around 3 months, it may not be worth continuing.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Extended-release formulation; exposure increases with high-fat meals (avoid high-fat meals with dosing)
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Not listed in the provided notes; refer to individual agents
pharmacokinetics.onset: Appetite/craving changes often start during the weekly titration phase; tolerance to nausea may improve over the first few weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Not listed in the provided notes; refer to individual agents
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Not listed in the provided notes; refer to individual agents
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: 12-hour extended-release tablets; typically dosed twice daily after titration
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Do not take with high-fat meals due to increased systemic exposure of both components

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Contrave is FDA-approved for chronic weight management (with diet + exercise). It is NOT approved for major depressive disorder or other psychiatric disorders—even though it contains bupropion (an antidepressant ingredient). In psychiatry, the most relevant use-case is when weight/metabolic health is part of the mental health picture (for example, weight gain on psych meds), but that’s not the official indication.
items: Chronic weight management: adjunct to reduced-calorie diet + increased physical activity
Eligibility (typical): BMI ≥30 kg/m², or BMI ≥27 kg/m² with at least one weight-related comorbidity (eg, dyslipidemia)
Treatment continuation check: consider stopping if <4% to 5% weight loss after ~3 months
off_label: Weight gain in people taking psychiatric medications (clinical practice consideration, not FDA-approved)
Reward-driven cravings / compulsive overeating patterns (not FDA-approved for binge eating disorder)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This combo hits appetite, reward, and energy—so the experience can feel like “less cravings,” “more drive,” or “too wired.” Here’s how people often describe it:

quotes: I still got hungry, but the urge to keep eating wasn’t running the show.
It didn’t kill appetite completely—it just made it easier to stop.
I felt more get-up-and-go in the morning.
My brain felt a little sharper—like I could actually start things.
It gave me a push… but sometimes it was too much push.
items.note: If you’re prone to anxiety or insomnia, this “activation” can backfire.

quotes: Falling asleep was harder the first couple weeks.
I felt wired at night if I took it too late.
My sleep got choppy until my body adjusted.
items.note: Timing matters: morning + evening dosing is standard, but late-evening dosing can worsen insomnia.

quotes: I felt kind of buzzy—like too much coffee.
My patience got shorter for a while.
Anxiety spiked early on, then settled down.
items.note: If anxiety, agitation, panic symptoms, or mood swings ramp up, that’s a real signal to reassess—not something to ignore.

quotes: Nausea was the main event at first.
The first weeks felt rough, then it eased up.
My pain meds didn’t work the way they normally do.
I learned the hard way you cannot mix this with opioids.
The label isn’t dramatic—opioid withdrawal is brutal.
items.note: If you use opioids (even intermittently), this medication can be unsafe.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Contrave is titrated up weekly, so the “effect” usually ramps rather than hitting all at once. The weight loss is gradual, but side effects (especially nausea, insomnia, jitteriness) can show up early.
key_points: Week 1: Many people notice nausea, headache, insomnia, or a “wired” feeling before they notice major craving changes
Weeks 2-4: Appetite/craving effects often become more noticeable as dosing increases
First 1-2 months: Highest-risk window for mood worsening or suicidal thoughts (especially in younger adults) and for anxiety/insomnia flare-ups
Around 3 months: If you haven’t lost ~4-5% of baseline weight, it may not be the right tool—discuss stopping

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Contrave isn’t meant to be a “take it forever no matter what” medication. A common approach is: if you’re not down roughly 4-5% of your starting weight after about 3 months, it may not be worth staying on it.
sections.clinical_details: Clinicians often use early response to guide whether the benefits outweigh side effects. This is especially important in psychiatry-adjacent use, because activation (insomnia, anxiety, irritability) can be a dealbreaker even if appetite improves.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If mood worsens or suicidal thoughts show up—especially early on or with dose changes—treat it as urgent.
sections.black_box: Contrave is not approved for treating depression or other psychiatric disorders, but it contains bupropion (an antidepressant ingredient). Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term trials. There was no increased risk seen in adults over 24, and risk was reduced in adults 65 and older. Monitor all patients closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts/behaviors, and unusual behavior changes, especially during the first 1-2 months or during dose adjustments. Families and caregivers should watch closely and communicate with the prescriber. Contrave is not approved for pediatric patients.
other: Opioids + Contrave: dangerous. Naltrexone blocks opioids and can precipitate withdrawal. Attempts to override the blockade can lead to fatal overdose.
Seizure risk: bupropion lowers seizure threshold. Dose must be increased gradually, and certain conditions/meds raise risk further.
Avoid in eating disorder history (bulimia/anorexia): seizure risk is higher.
Blood pressure/heart rate can rise: contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension; monitor regularly.
Neuropsychiatric reactions have occurred with bupropion (mood changes, agitation, psychosis, hostility, anxiety, panic, suicidality) in people with and without prior psychiatric illness.
Mania/hypomania risk: antidepressant-like activation can trigger mood switching in bipolar-spectrum patients.
patient_counseling: Do not take if you use opioids (including buprenorphine or methadone) unless your prescriber has clearly planned a safe opioid-free interval.
If you feel more agitated, panicky, sleepless, impulsive, or your mood gets darker—tell your prescriber immediately. Don’t tough it out.
Take exactly as titrated. Do not double doses if you miss one. Do not take more than 2 tablets at a time.
Avoid high-fat meals with dosing. This can increase medication exposure and side effects.
Know your seizure risk: history of seizures, eating disorders, heavy alcohol use, or abrupt sedative withdrawal makes this medication unsafe.
Check blood pressure before starting and periodically after—especially in the first 3 months.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: nausea, constipation, headache, dizziness, and sleep problems. Psych-relevant side effects include insomnia, anxiety/jitteriness, irritability, mood changes, and (rarely) severe neuropsychiatric symptoms.
plain_language_list: Anxiety or jitteriness (can happen, especially early)

common.patient_note: This is the top complaint. It often hits early during titration and may fade over time. Taking it as directed (and not with high-fat meals) can help.
Hydration, fiber, and a simple bowel plan matter. If constipation is severe or painful, don’t ignore it.
Often shows up during dose changes. If headaches are severe, persistent, or paired with high blood pressure symptoms, get checked.
This can feel like trouble falling asleep, waking up early, or “light sleep.” If you’re already an anxious/insomniac type, this side effect can be the dealbreaker.
Can be worse if you’re dehydrated, not eating regularly, or sensitive to activation. Stand up slowly; report presyncope/fainting.
Bupropion can feel activating. Mild activation can be manageable; escalating panic, agitation, or aggressive irritability is a stop-and-reassess moment.
Any new or worsening depression—especially with suicidal thoughts—needs prompt attention, particularly during the first 1-2 months or after dose changes.

serious: Suicidal thoughts/behavior (highest monitoring need in younger adults and during dose changes): urgent evaluation required
Seizures (dose-related risk from bupropion): permanently discontinue if seizure occurs
Severe neuropsychiatric reactions (rare): psychosis, hallucinations, paranoia, severe agitation, hostility, homicidal ideation—stop medication and seek urgent care
Hypertensive reactions or significant BP/HR increases: evaluate promptly
Acute opioid withdrawal (if opioids are in the system): can be severe; avoid unsafe opioid overlap
Hepatotoxicity (naltrexone-related reports): stop if signs/symptoms of hepatitis develop
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (rare): anaphylaxis/angioedema; severe skin reactions reported with bupropion

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: This medication is a combo of an opioid blocker (naltrexone) and an activating antidepressant ingredient (bupropion). Interactions matter—especially anything that affects opioids, seizure risk, or monoamine systems.

items.with: Opioids (including buprenorphine, methadone, and opioid pain medications)
items.risk: Can precipitate acute opioid withdrawal and block opioid analgesia. Attempts to overcome blockade with high opioid doses can cause fatal overdose.
items.action: Avoid opioid use. If opioid therapy is required, stop Contrave under prescriber guidance. If opioids are restarted after naltrexone exposure, lower doses may have stronger-than-expected effects—overdose risk is real.

items.with: MAOIs (and within 14 days of MAOI use)
items.risk: Serious interaction risk with bupropion; contraindicated. Also contraindicated when initiating Contrave in patients receiving linezolid or IV methylene blue (MAOI-like effects).
items.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting Contrave, and 14 days between stopping Contrave (bupropion) and starting an MAOI.

items.risk: Excess bupropion exposure increases seizure risk and adverse effects.
items.action: Contraindicated. Do not combine with Wellbutrin (any formulation), Aplenzin, Zyban, or any other bupropion product.

items.with: Alcohol (especially heavy use or withdrawal risk)
items.risk: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold. Abrupt alcohol discontinuation is a seizure risk state and is a contraindication scenario.
items.action: Avoid if you’re at risk for alcohol withdrawal. Be honest about drinking patterns before starting.

items.with: Medications/conditions that raise seizure risk (some antipsychotics, antidepressants, theophylline, systemic corticosteroids, hypoglycemic agents)
items.risk: Additive seizure risk and activation side effects (jitteriness, insomnia).
items.action: Risk-screen carefully. Dose titration must be gradual; avoid stacking multiple seizure-threshold-lowering agents when possible.

items.risk: Significantly increases systemic exposure of bupropion and naltrexone, increasing adverse effect risk.
items.action: Do not take with high-fat meals.
Avoid combination in settings where this applies.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Contrave is not a serotonergic antidepressant, so classic SSRI-style discontinuation symptoms are less likely. Still, if you’ve been on it for a while, tapering helps you monitor what returns (cravings, appetite, mood, energy, sleep) and reduces the chance of “rebound” discomfort.
key_points: If therapy has lasted ≥4 weeks: consider tapering over ~2 to 4 weeks so you can detect reemerging symptoms and avoid abrupt shifts in sleep/mood/appetite.
If therapy lasted 2 to 3 weeks: tapering over ~1 to 2 weeks is reasonable.
If therapy lasted <2 weeks: a taper is often not necessary, but discuss with your prescriber if you had strong activation (insomnia/anxiety) or other significant side effects.
Withdrawal symptoms from abrupt discontinuation are less likely than with serotonergic antidepressants because bupropion has minimal serotonergic activity.
If stopping because of serious psychiatric symptoms (suicidality, mania, psychosis, severe agitation): stopping sooner may be necessary—this should be clinician-guided.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Contrave uses a weekly step-up schedule to reduce side effects and lower seizure risk. After titration, the typical maintenance is twice daily dosing. Do not take with high-fat meals. Do not take more than 2 tablets at a time.

adult.weight_management_initial: Week 1: 1 tablet (naltrexone 8 mg/bupropion 90 mg) PO once daily in the morning
adult.weight_management_titration: Increase weekly as tolerated: Week 2: 1 tablet PO BID; Week 3: 2 tablets AM + 1 tablet PM; Week 4 and onward: 2 tablets PO BID
adult.weight_management_max: Maximum 4 tablets/day total (naltrexone 32 mg/bupropion 360 mg per day); no more than 2 tablets per dose

sections.simple_explanation: This med is built to ramp up slowly. The slow weekly increase is there for a reason: it reduces side effects and helps lower seizure risk. If you miss doses, don’t “catch up” by doubling—just restart safely with your prescriber’s guidance.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Weight-loss medications aren’t recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Psychiatric considerations matter here too: mood stability and sleep are already vulnerable in these stages, and this medication can be activating. Use extra caution in older adults and in people with kidney or liver impairment.
sections.pregnancy: Not recommended during pregnancy. Weight loss offers no clinical benefit in pregnancy and may cause fetal harm; discontinue if pregnancy is detected. Information on this specific combination in pregnancy is limited.
sections.lactation: Not recommended while breastfeeding. Naltrexone, bupropion, and metabolites are present in breast milk; due to safety concerns, weight-loss medications are generally avoided during lactation.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressant-class suicidality warning applies to children and adolescents; avoid.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing, but use caution. Older adults may be at greater risk of drug accumulation during chronic dosing and may be more sensitive to insomnia, blood pressure increases, dizziness, and neuropsychiatric effects.
sections.hepatic: Mild impairment: no dosage adjustment necessary. Moderate impairment: maximum 1 tablet PO BID. Severe impairment: use is not recommended.
sections.renal: Mild impairment: no dosage adjustment necessary. Moderate or severe impairment: maximum 1 tablet PO BID. End-stage renal disease: use is not recommended.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood and suicidality: screen for worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, and unusual behavior changes—especially in the first 1-2 months and during dose increases/decreases
Activation symptoms: anxiety, panic symptoms, agitation, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia-like restlessness
Bipolar risk: screen for bipolar disorder before starting; monitor for hypomania/mania (decreased sleep need, racing thoughts, risky behavior, grandiosity)
Sleep: insomnia severity, sleep fragmentation, and daytime fatigue (sleep disruption can destabilize mood)
Blood pressure and heart rate: baseline and periodic monitoring; risk may be higher during the first 3 months
Weight and BMI: track response and tolerability; reassess continuation at ~3 months
Blood glucose: baseline and periodic in patients with diabetes; watch for hypoglycemia if weight loss improves insulin sensitivity
Kidney and liver function: baseline and periodic, especially in patients with known impairment
Opioid status: confirm opioid-free interval when relevant; counsel about blocked analgesia and overdose risk if attempting to override blockade
Adverse effects that change functioning: dizziness, cognitive changes, tremor, severe nausea/dehydration, mood symptoms affecting daily life

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Contrave is a fixed-dose extended-release tablet. You can’t “custom mix” the ratio, and you shouldn’t crush or chew it.
items: Extended-Release Tablet (12-hour): naltrexone HCl 8 mg / bupropion HCl 90 mg
Administration: Typically taken twice daily (morning and evening) after titration; do not cut, chew, or crush
Food note: Do not take with high-fat meals

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Contrave combines two mechanisms: naltrexone blocks opioid receptors (which can reduce reward signaling tied to cravings), and bupropion weakly inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake (which can affect motivation, reward, and appetite pathways). The exact neurochemical path to weight loss isn’t fully nailed down, but the big targets are the hypothalamus (appetite regulation) and the mesolimbic dopamine circuit (reward system).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry-adjacent care, Contrave shows up when weight and cravings are harming health—and especially when weight gain is tangled up with psychiatric meds or mood-related eating. But it’s not a “mood med,” and it can destabilize sleep and anxiety in the wrong person. It’s a bad fit for anyone with opioid use, uncontrolled blood pressure, seizure risk, or eating disorder history. If a patient has bipolar-spectrum risk, you treat that risk seriously before using anything with antidepressant-like activation.

seo.title: Contrave (Naltrexone/Bupropion): Psychiatric Warnings, Side Effects, Dosing & Opioid Risks
seo.description: Contrave is a weight-loss medication (naltrexone/bupropion ER) with major psych-relevant warnings: suicidality monitoring, insomnia/anxiety activation, bipolar switching risk, and dangerous opioid interactions. Includes titration dosing, side effects, and safe discontinuation.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Contrave is not approved to treat depression. But it contains bupropion—the same active ingredient used in some antidepressants (like Wellbutrin). That means it can feel activating (more energy, less appetite, more drive) and it can also worsen insomnia, anxiety, or irritability in some people.

faqs.q: Can Contrave help anxiety or depression?
faqs.a: It’s not approved for anxiety or depression, and it’s not prescribed as a primary psychiatric treatment. Some people notice mood/energy changes because of the bupropion component, but others feel worse (more anxious, more wired, more irritable). If you’re struggling with mood symptoms, treat that directly with your clinician rather than hoping Contrave will “cover it.”

faqs.q: Why does Contrave have a suicidality warning?
faqs.a: Because it contains bupropion, which is also used in antidepressants. In short-term trials, antidepressants increased suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults. That’s why the key rule is: monitor closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts, or unusual behavior changes—especially early in treatment and during dose changes.

faqs.q: Can Contrave trigger insomnia or feeling “too wired”?
faqs.a: Yes. Insomnia and sleep disturbance are common. Some people also feel jittery, restless, or more anxious—especially during the weekly titration period. If sleep falls apart, mood often follows, so this isn’t a minor side effect for mental health—it can be a dealbreaker.

faqs.q: Is Contrave safe if I have bipolar disorder?
faqs.a: Use caution. Anything with antidepressant-like activation can trigger hypomania/mania in bipolar-spectrum patients. If there’s bipolar risk, your clinician should screen carefully first and monitor for red flags: less need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior, or unusually elevated/irritable mood.

faqs.q: Can I take Contrave if I use opioid pain meds or take buprenorphine/methadone?
faqs.a: No—this is one of the biggest safety issues. Naltrexone blocks opioids and can trigger withdrawal if opioids are in your system. It can also make opioid pain meds not work. And trying to override the blockade by taking more opioids is dangerous and can lead to fatal overdose.

faqs.q: What’s the dosing schedule for Contrave?
faqs.a: It’s a weekly step-up: Week 1 is 1 tablet in the morning. Week 2 is 1 tablet twice daily. Week 3 is 2 tablets in the morning and 1 in the evening. Week 4 and beyond is 2 tablets twice daily (max 4 tablets/day). Don’t take more than 2 tablets at one time.

faqs.q: How do I know if Contrave is working?
faqs.a: A common checkpoint is around 3 months: if you haven’t lost about 4-5% of your starting weight, it may not be worth continuing—especially if side effects are significant.

Abrupt discontinuation symptoms are less likely than with serotonergic antidepressants, but tapering is still reasonable if you’ve been on it for a while—mainly so you can track what returns (sleep issues, cravings, mood changes) and avoid a rough rebound. If you’re stopping due to serious psychiatric symptoms, your clinician may recommend a faster stop.

faqs.q: Does Contrave raise blood pressure or heart rate?
faqs.a: It can. It’s contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension. Blood pressure and heart rate should be checked before starting and monitored periodically—especially in the first 3 months.

faqs.q: Who should NOT take Contrave from a psychiatric safety standpoint?
faqs.a: People with seizure risk, eating disorder history (bulimia/anorexia), uncontrolled hypertension, heavy alcohol use with withdrawal risk, or bipolar-spectrum risk without proper screening/monitoring. And anyone using opioids should avoid it due to the naltrexone component.
